title: An accountant who left the ledger for the leaderboard has a workout plan for business owners to get in financial shape
summary: Matt Wilpers on how his years as an accountant set the foundation for his next act, and his advice for business owners and the accountants who serve them as they strive for success.
body_markdown:
“The power of the accountant is that you’re on the ground floor," said Matt, who spent time at a top public accounting firm before going in-house at an investment bank. "If you're in audit, you're seeing how things make it from the point of transaction all the way to the financial statements. And if you're on more of the bookkeeping or controlling side, you're performing analysis to help leadership make better decisions."


Matt loved setting goals, solving problems, and guiding decisions, but he didn't love the repetitive, manual desk work it often took to get there. When he started moonlighting as an athletic coach, that tension only grew more obvious.


“My passion was really in the fitness space. I was coaching at 5 in the morning in Central Park—it could be rain, snow, you name it—and then getting dressed at the gym to go to the office,” Matt recalled. “At work, they all thought I was crazy.”


But those early mornings were building on Matt’s accountant background, not bucking it. “In accounting, there are many parts of the job people don't necessarily see.”.


The ability to communicate, for example, was paramount. Whether he was writing emails or documenting processes and procedures, he needed to


[translate complex financials](https://quickbooks.intuit.com/r/growing-a-business/big-data-for-small-businesses/) into something business leaders could actually understand and act on.


"That's a skill I learned on the job when I was an accountant that I value today," said Matt. "When I'm coaching clients, I need to clearly communicate goals, track their progress, and plan for their future milestones."


## From spreadsheets to the leaderboard


When Matt finally took the plunge into full-time fitness coaching, he was still doing the same thing he'd always done: giving individualized advice, and building systems for consistent, compounding gains.


"When I left my career in accounting, it was like jumping off a cliff," he said. "You put so much time, schooling, and energy into becoming a CPA. Leaving that identity behind was difficult."


But shedding the identity didn't dull the instincts underneath it. His "consistency over intensity" philosophy, creating small, sustainable habits instead of sporadic sprints, is really the same principle behind a clean monthly close. The emphasis on getting the fundamentals right has kept showing up as he's built his own business. "As soon as I identify something that works, I make it a routine. I immediately try to figure out an efficient system or process to deal with it, and then I rely heavily on those established fundamentals going forward."
